title: DuckStation lets a post-processing stage sleep without forgetting its tuning
summary: Per-shader enable switches preserve chain order and custom parameters, separating temporary bypass from destructive removal in both Qt and FullscreenUI.
heroAlt: Source evidence from DuckStation pull request #3621: Qt, FullscreenUI, PostProcessing: Add shader enable/disable toggle.

sourceLabels.duckstation-pr-3621: Qt, FullscreenUI, PostProcessing: Add shader enable/disable toggle.

blocks.text: Removing a shader was the only way to bypass it

A post-processing chain often contains several effects whose parameters were tuned together. Before pull request #3621, temporarily checking the image without one stage meant removing it, then recreating the shader and its values later. That turns a simple comparison into configuration work and makes it easy to lose a carefully tuned preset or restore the effect in the wrong position.
Enabled state becomes part of the stage, not an empty replacement

The shared post-processing representation now records whether an individual shader executes. A disabled stage remains in the chain with its parameter values and ordering intact; the renderer simply skips its work. Re-enabling it therefore restores the same effect rather than creating a default instance. This differs from removing a stage, which remains the correct operation when the user wants the chain definition itself to change.
Qt and FullscreenUI expose the same non-destructive control

The implementation spans the post-processing utility layer, the Qt settings widget, and FullscreenUI settings. That ensures the enabled flag is not a frontend-only decoration: either interface edits the state the renderer consumes. It also lets users configure the same chain from a desktop window or controller-first display without one side silently dropping the new property.
Persistence and chain-order tests matter more than one screenshot

Create a chain with several shaders, modify multiple parameters, and disable a stage in the middle. Output should match a chain that skips that effect while later stages remain in the same order. Save settings, restart, and confirm the disabled state and parameters survive; then re-enable and compare against the original capture. Test both frontends, preset import, stage removal, and rapid toggling. GPU timing should fall only by the work of the bypassed stage.
Disable is now a reversible execution choice; remove remains a structural edit to the post-processing chain.
